chapter_theme: The last farewell: the palace falls silent as Civakan prepares to renounce, he teaches the weeping wives that wealth ends at the burning ground and that even the fruit of good deeds binds, they take off their ornaments and choose penance, and after giving away all he has he worships his mother and is carried off by the gods.

2974.reading: In the palace the lute, the drum and the women's song fall silent, the women's jasmine garlands crushed at their breasts, and the singing that was like sweet honey is gone.
2974.nuance: The verse gives no cause for the silence; the following verses supply it, the king's coming departure.

2975.reading: The whole city falls hushed as if asleep, and the roar like a dark sea that filled it is hidden.

2976.reading: The palace of the bowman-chested king, with its women and its drums, can teach what the unsteady world is like to anyone who has not yet understood it.
2976.nuance: The line 3 phrase தெருள்கலாதாய் is read here as 'to one who has not yet understood'; the verse turns the palace's splendour into a lesson.

claims.claim: the world is unstable and its pleasures do not stay

2977.reading: The smoke of hair-incense, of oblations, of lifted cloth and of garlands is gone, vanished like the fame of misers who give nothing of what they have gathered.
2977.nuance: வேள்விக் கொழும்புகை may be oblation smoke of a household rite; the verse does not name a school for it and uses it only as one of the things that vanish.

claims.claim: those who never give what they have gathered leave no fame behind

2978.reading: The neighing of the grass-eating horses, the cries of the conch-cutters and the herons, the careless laughter of young boys and the trumpet of the killer elephant and the conch all cease.

2979.reading: Flowers, garlands, sandal and ornaments, and the drink of honey that the women guarded, lose their hold and are no longer wanted, as the words of a text lose their sense for those who do not value it.
2979.nuance: Line 4's simile (சொற்பொருள்போல்) is hard: the sense may be that things are dropped like words of no concern; the reading here is a best guess.

2980.reading: The parrot forgets the sweet milk, the gods' offerings stop, the elephants no longer eat sugarcane, speech halts and all become strangers, and the city turns to a forest in the dark of night.

2981.reading: As the king prepares to renounce before the great lord, the wealth of the land that rolled like the roaring sea passes to the young ones and the city and country come to the feet of the strong one.
2981.nuance: Who is 'the great lord' (திருமால்) and who 'the strong one' (உரவோன்) is not fixed in the Tamil; the reading takes the first as Civakan and the second as his heir. The sons are not named.

2982.reading: With eyes red and long like spearheads set in the forge's flame, the women weep in grief, and the king speaks to them.
2982.nuance: The last line introduces the speech that fills the next verses.
2982.event: Civakan speaks to the weeping wives, beginning his teaching to them.

2983.reading: The king tells them that if the whole earth and sea were set against good penance they would not equal it, and that Fortune, who never leaves the one who knows that even a world of wealth is short of that and so lets go, will never reach the one who holds on with attachment.
2983.nuance: The Tamil of lines 1 to 4 is dense and the logic of 'never leaves' against 'never clings' reads as a paradox: wealth comes to the unattached. In the first ilampakam Fortune had left the clinging king (232).
2983.event: Civakan teaches the wives the worth of penance over wealth.

claims.claim: good penance outweighs all the wealth of the world
Fortune stays with the one who lets go and never clings to the one who holds on

2984.reading: Civakan asks if they want wealth that ends with unsalted rice poured by an outcaste in the burning ground, a rice-ball overturned on the bier and a wife smearing the house with her eye-black tears, and bids them listen.
2984.nuance: வெள்ளின் in line 2 is read as the bier-frame; the picture of the funeral is pieced together from rare words and cannot be fixed exactly.
2984.event: Civakan sets before the wives the funeral to which wealth leads and asks them to hear him.

claims.claim: wealth ends at the burning ground with a funeral and a widow's tears

2985.reading: Civakan says that even the lion that looks at the elephant may at the end sit beneath death, and that unless one crosses the flood of many deeds and drinks undivided bliss, one is bathing in the poison called the fruit of good deeds.
2985.nuance: The Jain view that merit as well as sin binds is stated strongly: நல்வினை விளையுள் is poison. Compare the sermon at 2846 where release is freedom from deeds.
2985.event: Civakan teaches that even good deeds have a fruit that binds.

claims.claim: the fruit of good deeds is itself poison; undivided bliss comes only by crossing the flood of deeds

2986.reading: Civakan says that if their children lack the great penance the guarded gems and gold will not follow them, and that the wealth of the sea-girt earth belongs to those who do penance, so they should do it.
2986.nuance: Line 1 is hard: ஆற்றிய மக்கள் என்னும் அருந்தவம் is read as 'the great penance called children'; the sense may be otherwise.
2986.event: Civakan urges the golden-adorned wives to take up penance.

claims.claim: gems and gold do not follow the dead
the wealth of the earth is for those who do penance

2987.reading: The long-eyed women's hearts, muddied by the clay of love, are cleared when the garlanded king stirs and settles them with disgust, and they say they will do great penance, though still held by the fetter of love for him.
2987.nuance: The verse's own image is of muddy water cleared by a stirrer; love for the husband is named the fetter that still binds the women as they decide.
2987.event: Civakan's teaching clears the wives' minds and they decide to take up penance.

claims.claim: disgust for pleasure clears a mind muddied by love

2988.reading: Civakan calls the wives to cross the old deeds, leave the famed rebirth and come with him if they want the secure bliss at the top of the golden world above.
2988.nuance: The summit of the world above is the Jain siddha abode; the verse says nothing of a god who grants it.
2988.event: Civakan invites the wives to renounce with him and reach release.

claims.claim: crossing old deeds leads to bliss at the top of the world above

2989.reading: The wives answer that to cling to pleasure now would be like gouging out one's eyes to watch a dance or throwing nectar from a jewelled vessel into the ash, and tell the crowned one that they will renounce.
2989.nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are hard: the images of gouged eyes and ash-covered nectar are read as the wives' own comparison, but the Tamil is unclear on who does these things.
2989.event: The wives accept Civakan's call and declare they will renounce.

claims.claim: clinging to pleasure destroys the very thing pleasure is sought for

2990.reading: The wives bow to the king whose hair they used to serve with flowers and ask him not to be angry when they come in the world he reaches to serve him as today.
2990.event: The wives bow to Civakan and ask to serve him in the world he goes to.

claims.claim: a wife may follow and serve her husband in the world beyond

2991.reading: The king of kings, having crossed the clear flood of the sea of learning, sees the pearl-garlanded women and entrusts them to the care of Vijayai, wise in lore.
2991.nuance: 'Care' is read from அபயம் வைத்தான், which can also mean he gave them a promise of safety; the verse does not state that they join her order, though the story elsewhere has her renounce.
2991.event: Civakan places his wives under his mother Vijayai's protection.

2992.reading: The wives lay aside their jewelled ornaments, like the wishing-tree branch and the vine of desire shedding the flowers that they themselves strip.
2992.nuance: The vine of desire (காமவல்லி) is the image: what had been the plant of desire is shown shedding its own flowers.

2993.reading: Under the pearl canopy on the gem floor the garlanded women, wishing that this may be theirs for seven births, wrap their breasts and brows in cloth while the god of love is said to beat his eyes and grieve.
2993.nuance: The last two lines are obscure and the reading is tentative: it may be the women wishing 'may we have this for seven births' or the jewels falling away.
2993.event: The wives put on the renunciant's cloth as the god of love mourns.

2994.reading: With perfume smoke, musk and powders put aside and the fragrant garlands of their hair taken off, the women become golden vines of virtue.
2994.nuance: The vine image (குணக்கொடி) turns the women into plants of virtue as they strip themselves of the scents of desire.
2994.event: The wives strip off their perfumes and garlands and become renunciants.

2995.reading: The king's bangled hands pour out the gifts to those who ask because they are in great want, as if two gold conches were pouring gems.
2995.nuance: The giving here is the last act before renunciation, with nothing to be had in return for it.
2995.event: Civakan gives gifts to beggars before he leaves.

2996.reading: His generous hands pour out white vessels like gold-showering lotuses, so that the world may eat its fill.
2996.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (என்பரிந்து எரிதலை): the reading takes them as the plea of the world in hunger.
2996.event: Civakan gives out vessels of food and gold to all the world.

2997.reading: The king gives away the fine clothes, ornaments, garlands and sandal that the world enjoys with delight and becomes a grove of wishing trees that rain gems.
2997.event: Civakan gives his clothes, ornaments and garlands to the world.

2998.reading: Civakan worships and blesses Vijayai, whose tender arms put the bamboo to shame, and boards the red palanquin that the gods then lift and carry away.
2998.nuance: The palanquin that had carried the mothers to renunciation (2628) now carries the son, and the gods, not men, bear it.
2998.event: Civakan bows to his mother, boards the palanquin and is carried off by the gods.

links.note: 2977 compares the vanished smoke of incense and garlands to the fame of misers who gave nothing; Naladiyar 9 says the miser who guards his wealth is already counted as one who has lost it.
links.teaches: Together they show the miser losing twice, his goods in the Naladiyar and his name in the epic, so hoarding gets a fate in memory as well as in wealth.

gains.a: the simile of vanishing smoke gets its ground, that the miser is already counted as a loss
gains.b: the Naladiyar's loss of the hoarder gets a trace in memory, his fame disappearing like the smoke

links.note: Kural 333 tells the possessor of wealth to do at once what stays because wealth does not; 2983 adds that Fortune stays with the one who is not attached and never clings to the one who is.
links.teaches: The Kural treats wealth's going as a fact to act on, while the epic makes clinging the cause of its going, so a reader sees what each assumes about why wealth leaves.

gains.a: the verse's claim about Fortune and attachment gets the plainer rule that wealth by nature does not stay
gains.b: the Kural's rule gets a reason for the going: wealth is lost through the very clinging that tries to keep it

links.note: In 232 Fortune leaves the clinging king without a word; in 2983 Civakan says she never leaves the one who lets go.
links.teaches: The goddess of fortune who abandoned the grasping king in the first ilampakam is shown in the last to stay with the king who gives up, so the story's arc on wealth reverses.

links.note: 2985 calls the fruit of good deeds poison and says only crossing the flood of deeds gives bliss; Tirumanthiram 258 makes penance and virtue the boat that carries one across the sea of deeds.
links.teaches: Both see deeds as a sea to cross, but one holds virtue's fruit to be poison and the other makes virtue the boat, so the two disagree on whether good deeds help or only bind.

gains.a: the epic's claim that merit too binds meets a text that sets virtue and austerity as the crossing itself
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's boat of virtue meets the Jain view that its fruit is a poison to be crossed

links.note: 2846 says the three jewels burn the tree of deeds and release is freedom from deeds; 2985 applies this to Civakan's wives, saying even the fruit of good deeds is poison.
links.teaches: The sermon's doctrine of freedom from deeds is turned into advice to the wives, and it is made to include good deeds that the sermon does not single out.

links.note: 2984 sets wealth against the funeral rice and the wife's tears at the burning ground; Tirumanthiram 149 gives the man's public mansion, palanquin and three crores and then his silent going.
links.teaches: The Tirumanthiram shows a life of building and giving with no look back; the epic shows what the household is left with, so together they give the whole before and after.

gains.a: the funeral picture is set after a life like the man's, in which a mansion and palanquin were all in public view
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's man who did not turn back gets a household to leave, with a widow's tears and a funeral rice

links.note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the eight wives, who came in her dream as eight garlands on the king's crown, never to part; in 2987 they decide to renounce.
links.teaches: The dream's garlands that were never to part are parted by the story's end, showing the epic setting a mother's wish against the wives' own turn from the household.

links.note: 2727 has Civakan reflect that to subdue oneself in time, do penance and reach a world without affliction is better; in 2988 he speaks it to his wives and calls them to come.
links.teaches: The reflection made alone in the earlier chapter becomes an invitation, so the resolve is seen first as thought and then as something shared.

links.note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; 2988 calls the wives to cross old deeds and reach bliss at the top of the world above.
links.teaches: The Kural names the pride to be cut and the height, the epic names the deeds to be crossed and the place, so each gives what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the summit above the world gets a condition the verse does not state, the cutting of 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's higher world gets a location at the top of the universe and a means in crossing old deeds

links.note: 2988 has the wives cross old deeds by leaving the household and gives no god; Tirumanthiram 219 has the worshipped fire rise and burn the diseases of deeds.
links.teaches: One text frees from old deeds by the renouncer's own crossing, the other by a fire that burns them when worshipped, which is the split between Jain effort and Saiva rite.

gains.a: the call to cross old deeds on one's own meets a text where a worshipped fire does the burning
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's fire that burns deeds meets a rival route with no fire and no god

links.note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the wives never to part from the king; in 2991 he entrusts them to her as he goes.
links.teaches: The mother who wished the wives to stay with her son is the one who now receives them as he leaves, so the wish is kept in a changed form.

links.note: 2992 has the wives lay aside their ornaments like a vine shedding flowers; Siddhar 19 asks when the speaker will leave silk and gold ornaments and desire the feet.
links.teaches: The Siddhar's wish to leave ornaments is shown done by women who give them up, but without the god's feet as its aim.

gains.a: the stripping of ornaments gets an aim in a god's feet that the epic's scene never names
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to leave silk and gold gets a scene where it is carried out, with the cost to those who give up beauty

links.note: Kural 221 says giving to the destitute is true giving and the rest a loan with return; 2995 has the king give to those who ask in great want on the eve of leaving.
links.teaches: The king giving just before he leaves the world where any return could come is the case the couplet's test points to, so the epic shows the rule in its purest form.

gains.a: the farewell gift is shown to be of the kind the Kural calls true giving, with no return possible
gains.b: the Kural's test of no return gets a case where the giver leaves the world in which returns could come

links.note: In 2628 the matrons go in palanquins to renounce and the king is left; in 2998 he boards a palanquin himself and the gods carry it.
links.teaches: The palanquin of renunciation first carried the mothers by men, and now carries the son by gods, so the epic shows the same vehicle changing in meaning from parting to ascent.

links.note: In 2998 the king mounts a palanquin that the gods carry; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the land mount the burning ground's palanquin for the last time.
links.teaches: The same royal vehicle is a bier in one and a god-borne chair to release in the other, so the reader sees how renunciation and death can wear the same procession.

gains.a: the king's palanquin gets the contrast of the bier in which a king is carried to the burning ground
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's royal bier gets a counter-case where the royal palanquin leads to release

source_issues: 2974, 2975, 2976, 2979, 2983, 2984, 2985, 2986, 2988, 2991, 2993 and 2998 and other stanzas were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines in the core file.
2979 line 4, 2981, 2983, 2984, 2986, 2989, 2993 and 2996 carry rare words or syntax that cannot be fixed; the readings are marked uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who hears the sage
Civakan's eight wives, who renounce with him
the gods who carry Civakan's palanquin
